title: Bar and Line Graph Interpretation
summary: Reading grouped and stacked bar charts and single or multi-series line graphs: telling a segment from a total, reading a trend, and measuring change between two points.
learningObjectives: Tell a grouped bar from a stacked bar and read a single segment in each.
Read a line graph for trend, peak, trough, and rate of change.
Measure percentage change between two points on the same series.
Distinguish a period figure from a cumulative one.

blocks.title: What bars and lines are for
blocks.markdown:
A **bar chart** compares separate categories — branches, quarters, products. Bars can be **grouped** (two or three bars standing side by side for each category) or **stacked** (one bar split into coloured segments that add up to the bar's height).

A **line graph** shows how one quantity moves across an ordered scale, almost always time. Several lines on one grid compare series. The exam gives the picture; here the same numbers are given as a small table so you can practise the reading, which is the part that matters.
searchKeywords: bar chart compares categories grouped stacked
line graph movement over time
several lines compare series

blocks.title: Reading a bar chart
blocks.markdown:
- **Grouped bars**: each bar is its own value. Read the height directly; the group just places related bars together for comparison.
- **Stacked bars**: the whole bar is a total, and each segment is a part. A segment's value is the distance between its two boundary lines, not the height of its top edge.
- **Comparing across categories**: line up the same series (same colour) across the axis and read each height.
- **A missing value**: in a stacked bar, one segment can be found as the bar total minus the segments you can read.

blocks.title: Reading a line graph
blocks.markdown:
- **Trend**: is the line rising, falling, or flat over the stretch the question asks about?
- **Peak and trough**: the highest and lowest points; questions often ask for the month of the maximum or the gap between max and min.
- **Steepness is rate, not level.** A steep segment means a fast change; it does not mean the values are high. Two lines can cross — before the crossing one is higher, after it the other.
- **Period vs cumulative**: check the title. "Loans disbursed each month" is a period figure; "total loans disbursed so far" is cumulative and never goes down.

blocks.title: Change between two points
blocks.markdown:
To measure how a series moved from one point to another, use the earlier point as the base: (later value − earlier value) ÷ earlier value × 100.

A rise from 20 to 33 is (33 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 65 per cent. A fall from 66 to 60 is (60 − 66) ÷ 66 × 100 ≈ −9.09 per cent. For the gap between two series at the same point, just subtract one height from the other.
searchKeywords: change between two points earlier as base
rise and fall percentage on a series
gap between two series is a subtraction

blocks.title: Worked example: two loan series
blocks.markdown:
Loans disbursed, in ₹ crore:

| Month | Home | Auto |
| ----- | ---- | ---- |
| Jan | 40 | 20 |
| Feb | 44 | 25 |
| Mar | 55 | 22 |
| Apr | 50 | 30 |
| May | 60 | 27 |
| Jun | 66 | 33 |

**Q1. Total home loans disbursed over the six months.** 40 + 44 + 55 + 50 + 60 + 66 = 315 crore.

**Q2. Percentage increase in auto loans from January to June.** Base is January: (33 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 65 per cent.

**Q3. Ratio of home loans to auto loans in March.** 55 ÷ 22 = 2.5, i.e. 5 : 2.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.markdown:
- **Reading a stacked segment's top edge as its value** instead of the distance between its two boundaries.
- **Treating a steep line as a high value.** Steepness is the speed of change, not the level.
- **Mixing up period and cumulative** figures — a cumulative line that appears to "grow fast" may just be adding steady monthly amounts.
- **Comparing different series** across the axis by colour and misreading one bar for its neighbour.
- **Using the later point as the base** for a change between two points.
- **Ignoring the axis scale** — bars may start at a value other than zero, exaggerating differences.
searchKeywords: bar line graph mistakes
stacked segment top edge steep line high value
period cumulative confusion axis scale

blocks.title: Quick revision
blocks.markdown:
- Bar chart compares categories; grouped bars are separate values, stacked bars are a total split into parts.
- A stacked segment's value is the distance between its two boundaries; a missing segment is the bar total minus the rest.
- Line graph shows trend, peak and trough; steepness is rate of change, not level; lines can cross.
- Check period vs cumulative from the title.
- Change between two points divides by the earlier point; the gap between two series is a subtraction.

grouped stacked trend peak rate period cumulative recap

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a grouped bar chart and a stacked one?
flashcards.back: Grouped: two or three separate bars per category, each its own value. Stacked: one bar per category, split into segments that sum to the bar's total.
flashcards.explanation: In a stacked bar the whole height is a total, not a single value.

flashcards.front: How do you read the value of one segment in a stacked bar?
flashcards.back: Take the distance between its lower and upper boundary lines, not the height of its top edge. A missing segment = bar total minus the segments you can read.
flashcards.explanation: Reading the top edge gives a running subtotal, not the segment.

flashcards.front: On a line graph, what does a steep segment tell you?
flashcards.back: A fast rate of change over that stretch. It does not mean the values are high — a steep line can sit low on the axis.
flashcards.explanation: Two lines can cross; the higher one swaps at the crossing point.

flashcards.front: How do you tell a period figure from a cumulative one on a line graph?
flashcards.back: Read the title. 'Loans disbursed each month' is a period figure and can rise or fall; 'total loans disbursed so far' is cumulative and never decreases.
flashcards.explanation: A cumulative line rising steadily is just adding constant monthly amounts.

flashcards.front: How do you measure the change in one series between two points on a graph?
flashcards.back: (later value - earlier value) / earlier value x 100. The earlier point is the base.
flashcards.explanation: The gap between two different series at one point is just a subtraction.

flashcards.front: Why check where a bar chart's value axis starts?
flashcards.back: If it starts above zero, small differences between bars look much larger than they are. Read the numbers, not the relative bar heights.
flashcards.explanation: A truncated axis is a common way a chart misleads.

flashcards.front: How do you compare one series across categories in a grouped bar chart?
flashcards.back: Follow the same-coloured bar across the axis and read each height in turn, keeping clear of the neighbouring bar in each group.
flashcards.explanation: Misreading a bar for its group neighbour is a frequent slip.
